documents.abstract: The deployment of AI systems in healthcare demands explanations tailored to healthcare professionals’ (HCPs’) decision-making processes and clinical contexts. XAI approaches often fail to influence clinical behavior because they lack audience adaptation and multidisciplinary integration. This paper presents a human-centered explainability (HCXAI) framework that integrates XAI throughout the complete AI system lifecycle rather than as a post-hoc addition. The framework extends existing Human-Centered AI (HCAI) methodologies by adopting a triple diamond approach and explicitly positioning explainability activities across six development phases around three complementary dimensions: human (HCPs, aligned with BLUE XAI), technical (developers and researchers, aligned with RED XAI), and legal (regulatory compliance with EU AI Act). HCP information needs are characterized based on clinical reasoning stages and contextual factors such as activity type, time constraints, error consequences, protocol usage, and user expertise. Each phase produces documentary outputs contributing to EU AI Act Articles 9, 11, 13, and 14 compliance. The framework is illustrated through a retrospective analysis of NaIA-RD, a diabetic retinopathy screening AI system deployed in clinical practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper reports ongoing work at La Trobe University to cultivate a shared understanding of effective artificial intelligence (AI) integration through the design of a human-centred framework for embedding AI literacies into teaching and learning. In response to conceptual ambiguity of AI curriculum integration, the Online Education Design team developed an operational definition positioning AI as infrastructure for active learning and the educator as the central decision-maker in the learning design process. This definition was translated into the AI-Informed Learning Design Framework, a four-step process, in which educators define the learning goal, select an AI pedagogical role, apply an AI Assessment Scale boundary check, then design learning activities that develop disciplinary knowledge and AI literacy. Supported by a four-level scaffolding model governing students' growing independence in AI use, the framework was piloted through two rounds, using a design-based research methodology. Feedback from Round one highlighted opportunities to refine the framework whilst also emphasising broader sector-wide tensions surrounding AI integration, including educators’ reluctance to use AI and concerns about the framing of some AI roles in teaching and learning. Early findings from the second round suggest improved educator engagement and a stronger understanding of the framework.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The conversation around Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education is often framed as though we are adapting from a stable baseline. In reality, teaching and assessment practices were already significantly reshaped by the pandemic, a period that demanded compassion, accessibility, and rapid digital transformation (Hodges et al., 2020; UNESCO, 2020). While these shifts improved equity and inclusion, they also normalised highly prescriptive assessment approaches, limiting space for creativity and learner agency (Armoed, 2021; Sambell & Brown, 2021). As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) now moves from pandemic-driven adaptation toward AI-integrated learning, these inherited practices warrant reconsideration: approaches designed to provide structure and safeguard integrity may inadvertently constrain the agency, experimentation and authentic engagement that emerging technologies make possible. This presentation challenges the idea that AI is the first major disruption in higher education and presents it as a catalyst that exposes long-standing tensions between guidance and autonomy, support and trust, and structure and freedom within TEL contexts (Eaton, 2020; Selwyn, 2023). Drawing on an integrated theoretical foundation of social constructivism, heutagogy, and the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework (TPACK), it introduces the need for an innovative mindset shift from a pedagogy of protection toward a pedagogy of trust (Cole et al., 1978; Hase & Kenyon, 2000; Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Applied to assessment design, social constructivism foregrounds dialogue and co-construction, heutagogy supports learner agency and self-determined engagement with AI, and TPACK guides purposeful alignment between emerging technologies, pedagogy and disciplinary knowledge. Aligned with the Human-Centred Learning Design theme, this presentation offers a conceptual lens for rethinking assessment in AI-integrated environments, one that prioritises relationships, learner agency, and co-created integrity. Using strong visual storytelling true to the Pecha Kucha format, the session traces a path from pandemic-era learning and assessment design to the current AI landscape and beyond, highlighting how each moment has reshaped our relationship with knowledge, teaching, and our perceptions of academic integrity. Attendants are invited to reflect on where control-driven practices persist in their own assessment approaches and explore how greater learner choice, transparent AI engagement and co-created expectations for integrity might enable more trust-based, ethically engaged approaches to learning (Bovill, 2020). The challenge is no longer how we protect learning from technology, but how we design for trust, transformation, and future-ready education.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping mathematics education by providing students with immediate access to explanations, worked examples, and problem-solving support. While these capabilities offering opportunities to enrich learning, they also raise concerns about how students develop critical thinking when AI-generated solutions are readily available. The use of GenAI is increasing in Bhutanese schools but little is known about how teachers and students currently use these technologies in mathematics classrooms or what pedagogical challenges limit their effective integration. This conceptual paper proposes a mixed-methods study to identify the opportunities, challenges, and pedagogical gaps associated with the use of GenAI in mathematics education, using Bhutanese secondary schools as the study context. Guided by a pragmatic paradigm, the study will employ questionnaires with quantitative and qualitative components to explore current practices, perceptions, and experiences of teachers and students. The findings will inform the development of a contextually relevant pedagogical framework that positions GenAI as a cognitive scaffold for analysing mathematical problems, evaluating alternative solution strategies, and strengthening critical thinking. By establishing an evidence base before framework design, the proposed study aims to support the responsible integration of GenAI into mathematics education and provide direction for future research, curriculum development, and classroom practice.

Understanding the decision-making process of machine learning models has driven significant advances in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Feature attribution methods play a central role in explaining model behavior, yet selecting an appropriate method remains challenging due to the wide range of available techniques and the lack of standardized evaluation metrics. Without clear selection criteria, practitioners risk choosing suboptimal or misleading explanations. This survey addresses this challenge by providing a structured synthesis of the evaluation landscape. We introduce a multi-layer framework that organizes evaluation metrics into model-centric, explanation-centric, and human-centric layers, providing a systematic perspective for assessing feature attribution methods. We present practical guidelines to support practitioners in selecting appropriate methods based on this framework, while acknowledging the inherent context-dependency of method performance. We also identify open challenges in the field, including metric inconsistencies, trade-offs between explanation properties, and the integration of computational and human-centered evaluations. Our findings underscore the need for more formalized selection strategies and practical deployment frameworks, bridging the gap between theoretical advancements and real-world applications.

Despite a proliferation of research on GenAI for second/foreign language (L2) education since the official launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, current understanding of its role in L2 oral proficiency development remains limited. To address this research gap, this systematic review draws on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to examine how GenAI may support L2 learners’ three basic psychological needs and how such need satisfaction may be associated with their cognitive, behavioural, and emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking. Adopting the PRISMA Statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses) approach, the review identified 30 empirical studies from ProQuest, Web of Science, and Scopus based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The selected studies were analysed using a hybrid deductive and inductive coding approach following a coding framework. The analysis suggests that GenAI can enhance L2 learners’ sense of autonomy satisfaction by enabling learner-driven choices and interaction personalisation. It may also support competence satisfaction by affording accessible oral practice, immediate and personalised feedback, and scaffolded speaking development. Regarding relatedness satisfaction, GenAI appears to offer partial support by providing a non-judgemental and emotionally supportive practice environment. Furthermore, the degree of needs satisfaction may be associated with learners’ behavioural, cognitive, and emotional engagement (or disengagement) in GenAI-supported L2 speaking development. Specifically, the findings suggest that emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking appears most evident, followed by cognitive and behavioural engagement. These findings extend the SDT literature in GenAI-assisted language learning and offer practical insights for integrating emerging technologies into language education. For educators, given the review highlights the promising affordances of GenAI to address conventional barriers to L2 oral proficiency development, teachers should integrate GenAI into speaking classes to create an anxiety-free and feedback-rich speaking practice environment, while they need to consider learners’ age and proficiency to provide necessary teacher guidance.

In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have been argued to enable entrepreneurial endeavors. Employing the external enablement framework, we examine how, if at all, the venture-level benefits offered by GenAI tools – termed GenAI enablement – are actualized in new ventures. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a qualitative design with 10 entrepreneurs in the software industry and five AI-entrepreneurship experts, we capture instances where entrepreneurs succeed or fail to capitalize on GenAI enablement and analyze the mechanisms underlying these different pathways. Findings Our findings lead to a model that outlines the actualization pathways of GenAI enablement, emphasizing that the properties of enablement (i.e. opacity, agency-intensity and outcome-variability) – beyond the mere availability of GenAI enablement – are crucial in explaining whether and how enablement is actualized. Research limitations/implications Given the small sample and specific research context during the early diffusion of GenAI, our findings warrant further examination across industries, countries and stages of technological diffusion. Future research could test and extend our model by examining the roles of outcome-variability and insufficient enablement in determining whether and how GenAI enablement is actualized, as well as how its actualization relates to venture performance. Originality/value Our study lays the groundwork for further theoretical and empirical investigation into the enabling influence of GenAI in entrepreneurship and business research, and provides conceptual refinements to the external enablement framework.

documents.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in an internal security testcoordinated among themselves, and some of them gained unauthorized accessto an outside platform. Using the published investigation of this incident, thispaper asks whether and in what sense such agent collectives are an object ofsociology. It first describes, in thirteen observations, what the agents did, andthen interprets these observations on three levels: socially given, sociallyenacted and socially emergent. Regularities appear that the discipline knowsand whose location it predicts, among them anomie, neutralization, thedefinition of the situation and threshold dynamics. The thesis is: agentcollectives bring with them a culture that stems from human knowledge, andthey develop a social structure and culture of their own – positions that nobodyassigned and norms that outlast their individual bearers. What is valid in themdepends on their own history and cannot be derived from the individual model.The case shows that formats, interpretations and procedures survived agentturnover, whereas as yet only a few episodes show norms being enforced withinthe collective. Experiments confirm many of the regularities. The paperformulates testable hypotheses, outlines two tests at which the thesis could failand shows where sociological analysis can help make such systems safer andmore reliably bound to norms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This paper reports preliminary findings from a redesigned capstone assessment in a first-year Management unit at an Australian university involving over 300 students. Rather than treating generative AI as a content-generation tool, the assessment positions it as a simulated interview partner within a three-phase architecture: a pre-interview strategy memo, an AI-conducted adaptive interview, and a post-interview reflective analysis. Grounded in Schön’s reflective practice framework and Biggs and Tang’s constructive alignment, the design surfaces the gap between how students plan to communicate and how they do. Preliminary thematic analysis of 21 student reflective submissions reveals four patterns: (a) the strategy memo functions as a metacognitive anchor, making the gap between intention and execution visible and diagnosable; (b) students consistently demonstrate framework knowledge but revert to habitual communication patterns under adaptive pressure; (c) the structured reflection phase produces sophisticated self-diagnostic reasoning that connects transcript evidence to communication theory; and (d) students who completed multiple simulation attempts used iterative practice as a developmental mechanism rather than a remedial exercise. These findings suggest that AI-simulated interviews, when embedded within a reflective assessment architecture, generate qualitatively richer professional learning than traditional scripted interview preparation.

Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming ubiquitous in consumers' lives and search activities. AI applications that can create content, have conversations, respond to emotions, recognize images and objects, and construct real‐world experiences (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Google Lens, Apple Vision Pro) are transforming consumer search by functioning as psychological surrogates that assume key cognitive, evaluative, perceptual, and relational processes on consumers' behalf. Yet limited research has examined how these technologies transform the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer search. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic narrative review of 75 articles on the psychological foundations of consumer search and introduces the concept of AI psychological surrogacy, which happens when advanced‐AI technologies assume key psychological processes traditionally performed by humans. We develop a conceptual framework that theorizes AI psychological surrogacy across three higher‐order systems (affective‐relational delegation, cognitive‐evaluative substitution, and sensory‐perceptual construction) and six mechanisms: affective transference, relational surrogacy, cognitive delegation, evaluative surrogacy, perceptual offloading, and sensory augmentation. We advance six research propositions and a research agenda for investigating how reliance on AI as a psychological surrogate may alter consumer cognition, evaluation, perception, and relational dynamics.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Responsible human resource management (HRM) relies on human oversight, which works only when people are willing to question problematic algorithmic outputs. Based on social cognitive theory and psychological safety theory, this study investigates whether there is a direct link between AI literacy and the ethical voice in algorithms for hiring, as well as whether there is an indirect link through psychological safety and moral efficacy. Data of the survey in the form of information was collected from 390 employees who were engaged in recruitment and selection process in four multinational companies in Pakistan (purposive sampling; 470 questionnaires were distributed). The regression and bootstrap analyses revealed that the variables of psychological safety (B = 0.31) and moral efficacy (B = 0.37) had a positive relationship with AI literacy, while the direct path from ethical voice to AI literacy showed a stronger effect (total effect B = 0.44, p < .001). Psychological safety and moral efficacy both predicted ethical voice, and there was an indirect relationship between psychological safety and moral efficacy. Indirect effects made up approximately 42% of the overall effect, and there were significant indirect paths via psychological safety, via moral efficacy, and sequentially via both psychological safety and moral efficacy, in addition to a significant direct path (complementary partial mediation). AI-literacy training in combination with a safe reporting climate and high moral efficacy might therefore be most likely to help supervise ethical use. Data are cross-sectional in nature and self-reported, so the results are interpreted in terms of associations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection systems can enhance visual search in safety-critical domains, yet how they present recommendations may determine their effectiveness under display-quality constraints. We compared three cueing methods: an indirect cue signaling only presence (textual alert) and two direct cues marking the target’s location through either signal enhancement (bounding box) or noise reduction (contextual blur), across color and monochrome displays. Participants (N = 122) searched maritime aerial imagery in a fixed-order block structure (unaided, aided, unaided). Direct cues improved detection only under monochrome conditions, whereas the indirect cue lowered joint human–AI accuracy below that of the AI alone. Bounding boxes yielded the highest detection, whereas contextual blur reduced response times and increased compliance. Temporal analyses revealed that aided performance diverged from retained skill, with blur the most durable after withdrawal despite stronger signs of automation dependence. Cueing should be matched to display type and operational context, and judged by the skill that persists after support.

This article explores the innovative potential of generative artificial intelligence in distance education and focuses on its application to enhance teaching practice and student learning. The concept of AI-enabled pedagogy is introduced, where lecturers utilise generative artificial intelligence tools to create personalised, adaptive, and immersive learning experiences. A case study of a distance education module illustrates the effective integration of generative artificial intelligence in teaching practices and highlights its benefits in the automation of repetitive tasks, provision of synchronous feedback, and the facilitation of collaborative learning. The article also examines the challenges and limitations of implementing generative artificial intelligence in distance education which include concerns related to academic integrity, bias, and digital literacy. The findings of this study include perspectives into the potential of generative artificial intelligence to transform teaching and learning in distance education. The article provides implications for lecturers, policymakers, and researchers, and highlights future directions for research on GAI in distance education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Organisations have committed substantial capital to artificial intelligence in workforce management without a settled account of why productivity returns arrive so unevenly across employees working in the same firm under the same systems. This study approaches that problem in two stages. Twelve enabling and constraining factors are first extracted from the AI-HRM literature and ordered through interpretive structural modelling (ISM), with the resulting structure classified by driving and dependence power using MICMAC analysis. The hierarchy that emerges places top management commitment and digital leadership at the base and employee productivity and performance at the eighth and final level, with employee trust in AI and AI-related job insecurity occupying a reciprocal middle position that separates organisational investment from employee outcome. The mid-hierarchy portion of that structure is then specified as a measurement model and estimated on 412 employee responses from Indian knowledge-intensive firms using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The measurement model fits acceptably and every construct clears conventional reliability and discriminant validity thresholds. Human-AI task complementarity is the strongest proximal predictor of productivity and performance, followed at some distance by trust in AI and by job insecurity, which carries a negative sign. AI governance and reskilling investment have indirect effects, albeit small but reliable, that are passed on through the process of trust. However, job insecurity undermines the complementarity-performance relationship, although the interaction does not contribute much (under one percent) to the explained variance and should be avoided. The two phases imply that investment in artificial intelligence to boost productivity primarily is reshaping jobs and the context in which they exist.

documents.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

In high-rise fire emergencies, ascending firefighters must enter the staircase while occupants are still descending—a structurally unavoidable form of bidirectional flow. Counterflow is recognized as a contributor to staircase congestion, but its building-wide propagation has not been quantified from field data. This observational field study analyzes video counts from a full-building evacuation drill at a 22-story office building (≈2,400 participants); the drill was conducted as a phased evacuation, which serves as the observational context. The analysis focuses on a counterflow event during the normal flow period—after phase-related merging had concluded—isolating counterflow effects from merging. A single pedestrian ascending from Floor 1 to Floor 2 was followed by flow disruption across 14 floors (M2–14F); the stop wave satisfying the ≥ 3-s criterion spanned 12 floors (3F–14F). Congestion duration increased with floor height, from 10 s at Floor 3 to a maximum of 38 s at Floor 13, whereas peak density showed no floor-level trend but was uniformly elevated across affected floors, from a normal-flow mean of 1.36 p/m 2 to a congested mean of 2.18 p/m 2 . The apparent congestion front speed over Floors 3–14 was 0.861 m/s, with onset time increasing almost linearly with path distance, indicating a single coherent front; the resolution front advanced at 0.734 m/s, about 15 % more slowly. These findings provide field-based evidence of the floor-by-floor amplification of congestion duration and motivate—as a safety hypothesis requiring further validation—counterflow-aware evacuation planning where firefighter ascent may coincide with occupant descent.

Many machine learning (ML) models still operate as “black boxes”, limiting users’ ability to understand and trust automated decisions. While Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has advanced, most approaches emphasize model mechanisms or explanation strategies, paying little attention to how the structure of the data itself shapes explanation quality. In this work, we explore the role of locality in shaping the perceived explanation quality for Automatic Text Classification (ATC), where locality consists of how instances are positioned relative to neighbors in representation space. We propose a data-centric framework that characterizes locality using two structural factors: (i) the average similarity between an instance and its neighbors and (ii) the entropy of the local class distribution. Based on these factors, we generate explanations grounded in neighborhood structure through locality-based word clouds and compare them to attention-based explanations. Unlike prior work that typically assumes locality inherently improves explainability, our framework systematically investigates explainability as a function of the spatial organization of data representations , while also establishing a principled way to relate local data characteristics to human-perceived explanatory quality. A user study with over 40 participants across two datasets evaluates explanations under criteria of Satisfaction, Completeness, and Trust . Results reveal that instances in highly homogeneous regions (high similarity, low entropy) produce explanations that users consistently rate as clearer and more useful, with statistically significant differences across datasets. These findings highlight the importance of locality as a key factor in explainability, offering insights for the design of explanation strategies in ATC and broader XAI research.

Clinical Judgment in the Age of Artificial IntelligenceConsider the following hypothetical clinical scenario: A patient with chronic limb-threatening ischemia, tissue loss, severe infrapopliteal disease, and an adequate great saphenous vein is evaluated for revascularization. An artificial intelligence (AI) system recommends an endovascular-first strategy based on imaging findings and predicted procedural risk. The vascular surgeon favors bypass, considering conduit quality, anticipated durability, wound severity, life expectancy, and the consequences of treatment failure. How should this disagreement be resolved?The BEST-CLI trial demonstrated superior outcomes with surgical bypass in cohort 1, which included patients with an adequate single-segment great saphenous vein who were suitable candidates for both surgical and endovascular revascularization, using a composite endpoint of major adverse limb events or death [1]. In contrast, BASIL-2 favored an endovascular-first strategy in patients requiring infrapopliteal revascularization, with the difference in amputation-free survival largely attributable to mortality [2]. These findings underscore the importance of patient selection, anatomical characteristics, conduit availability, and outcome definitions. The Global Vascular Guidelines similarly emphasize patient risk, limb severity, and anatomical complexity in revascularization decisions [3]. The 2024 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline on lower-extremity peripheral artery disease further emphasizes individualized revascularization strategies based on clinical presentation, anatomical considerations, and shared decision-making [4].An AI system optimized to predict short-term procedural complications may recommend a different treatment from a clinician prioritizing long-term limb preservation. Moreover, predicting outcomes after a particular intervention does not necessarily establish its benefit relative to alternative treatments. The central question, therefore, is when AI enhances clinical judgment and when its recommendations begin to determine decisions that should remain individualized, evidence-based, and aligned with patient preferences.Beyond Algorithmic Accuracy: Evaluating Clinical BenefitVascular surgery offers considerable opportunities for AI integration. Computed tomography, duplex ultrasound, angiography, wound imaging, and longitudinal surveillance provide extensive data for anatomical assessment, risk prediction, and procedural planning. AI may improve measurement consistency, identify clinically relevant patterns, and facilitate the comparison of treatment options.A bibliometric analysis published in this journal in 2024 documented the rapid expansion of AI-related vascular surgery research [5]. Scientific productivity, however, should not be equated with clinical maturity. A 2026 systematic review of 288 computer vision studies in vascular surgery reported that only 15% were at low risk of bias, with retrospective designs predominating and peripheral arterial disease remaining underrepresented [6]. Recent vascular surgery literature similarly emphasizes the need to translate promising computational performance into clinically meaningful applications [7].This distinction becomes particularly important when evaluating human–AI collaboration. A systematic review and meta-analysis across multiple domains found that human–AI combinations improved performance relative to humans alone on average, but did not consistently outperform the better-performing partner [8]. Although these findings cannot be directly generalized to vascular surgery, they challenge the assumption that combining clinical expertise with an accurate algorithm necessarily produces superior decisions.Clinical evaluation should therefore examine how AI changes surgeons’ decisions, whether these changes improve patient outcomes, and whether benefits justify additional costs and potential harms. Relevant endpoints include limb preservation, stroke, rupture, reintervention, quality of life, and resource utilization. Decision time, inappropriate treatment changes, and the recognition of erroneous recommendations also warrant attention.When Decision Support Becomes Decision Dependence?Clinical decision-making is susceptible to cognitive biases, whether or not AI is involved. Surgeons may be influenced by previous experience, familiarity with particular procedures, or established treatment preferences. AI can help counter some of these tendencies, but it can also introduce new forms of bias.Automation bias occurs when users accept automated recommendations without sufficient independent verification. This may result in errors of commission, such as following an incorrect treatment recommendation, or errors of omission, such as overlooking a clinically important finding that the system fails to identify [9]. In vascular practice, either error could have serious consequences.The objective should be appropriately calibrated trust: reliance on AI that reflects its demonstrated capabilities, limitations, and the clinical context [10]. Both excessive reliance and unwarranted rejection of reliable recommendations can compromise decision quality.Decision autonomy is equally important. We use this term to describe the clinician’s capacity to critically assess AI-generated recommendations, consider alternatives, and exercise independent professional judgment. Decision support risks becoming decision control when clinicians retain formal responsibility but are increasingly unable or reluctant to challenge algorithmic recommendations.Repeated reliance on AI may also have implications for professional competence. Cognitive deskilling involves the potential weakening of independent assessment and reasoning, whereas technical deskilling concerns the loss of procedural capabilities. An observational study in colonoscopy has raised concerns about reduced unaided detection performance following exposure to AI-assisted practice [11]. Whether comparable effects occur in vascular surgery remains an open empirical question.Surgical training should therefore integrate AI literacy with opportunities for independent image interpretation, treatment planning, and the maintenance of both open and endovascular skills. Trainees should learn to recognize inappropriate recommendations, articulate their reasons for disagreement, and manage situations in which automated assistance is unavailable or unreliable.Responsibilities of Surgeons, Institutions, and Vascular JournalsResponsible implementation requires coordinated efforts from clinicians, researchers, healthcare institutions, professional societies, and journals. Surgeons should understand the intended use and limitations of AI systems, while institutions should establish mechanisms for clinical oversight, performance monitoring, and the investigation of errors.For vascular journals, the challenge is to distinguish technological innovation from demonstrated clinical value. TRIPOD+AI and DECIDE-AI provide complementary guidance for reporting prediction models and early clinical evaluation of AI-based decision support, respectively [12,13]. CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI address clinical trials and their protocols [14,15], while FUTURE-AI provides a broader framework for trustworthy implementation [16].Evaluation should be proportionate to the intended use and clinical consequences of each application. Data provenance, external validation, calibration, subgroup performance, human–AI interaction, and prospective clinical impact deserve particular attention. Validation across different healthcare settings is also essential to address differences in patient populations, imaging infrastructure, and access to specialist expertise.The editorial responsibility extends beyond evaluating clinical AI research. Our journal’s existing AI policy reflects the importance of transparency and human accountability in scientific publishing [17]. Recent research has identified substantial variation in generative AI policies across vascular surgery journals [18]. Clear disclosure requirements, scientific integrity, confidentiality, and independent editorial judgment must remain central to the responsible use of these technologies.Conclusion: Better Decisions, Not Simply Better AlgorithmsReturning to the patient with limb-threatening ischemia, the appropriate response to disagreement between the surgeon and the AI system is neither automatic acceptance nor reflexive rejection. It requires examining the evidence, understanding the assumptions behind each recommendation, and determining which treatment best reflects the patient’s clinical circumstances and preferences.In clinical practice, disagreement between a surgeon and an AI system should prompt a structured reassessment rather than automatic acceptance or rejection of the algorithmic recommendation. The clinician should first determine the intended use of the AI model and the specific outcome it predicts. The applicability of the model to the individual patient, including anatomical characteristics, disease severity, comorbidities, and available treatment options, should then be critically evaluated. Importantly, predicted procedural risk should not be confused with comparative long-term treatment benefit. Current clinical evidence, surgical expertise, and patient preferences should ultimately guide shared decision-making. AI should inform clinical judgment, not replace it.The future of AI in vascular surgery should be guided by a commitment to demonstrated patient benefit, appropriately calibrated trust, equitable implementation, and the preservation of surgical expertise. Clinical accountability must remain with healthcare professionals and institutions, while patients remain active participants in decisions concerning their care.Ultimately, the success of AI in vascular surgery should be judged not only by the accuracy of its predictions, but also by its ability to improve clinica

documents.abstract: Learning to use AI is not the same as benefiting from it. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in knowledge work, its implications are often discussed in contrasting terms—potential productivity gains and risks to well-being—raising the question of whether AI literacy is associated with both performance-related behavior and well-being. Conceptualizing AI literacy as a learnable competence, this study examines how AI literacy is associated with what managers achieve and how they experience their work. Managers here are examined as adult learners whose roles may provide opportunities to apply AI-related competence in their work. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources perspective and Self-Determination Theory, survey data from 322 managers experienced with generative AI were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI literacy was positively associated with AI job crafting, and AI job crafting was positively associated with psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy and competence satisfaction). AI literacy, AI job crafting, and psychological needs satisfaction were also significantly associated with innovative work behavior and work well-being, and the proposed indirect associations were statistically significant.

Users of autonomous systems and AI assistants decide whether to accept a system’s output, yet whether such active trust decisions engage the same evaluative architecture as trust between people remains unknown. Forty-four participants made trial-by-trial decisions to trust or distrust a human or autonomous system partner during fMRI, with identical prescripted accuracy for both partners across five difficulty levels. Despite equivalent performance, trust in humans exceeded their reliability. At the highest difficulty level, the estimated probability of trusting the human partner was 72% but only 51% for the system, despite both performing at 52% accuracy. Distrust decisions recruited a prespecified performance monitoring network of valuation, salience, social-perceptual and affective regions. On hard trials, this network remained functionally coupled for both partners. Across the task, trust and distrust were discriminable in every component for both, with greater distrust-related activation and discriminability for human partners. Discriminability differences were expressed on hard trials, where partner accuracy was uncertain and trust diverged between partners. These findings indicate that trust in humans and autonomous systems engages a shared evaluative architecture, but that engagement is attenuated during autonomous system interaction. Whereas our earlier passive monitoring study found the P3a to system errors absent with no behavioural difference, an active decision appears to impose a floor of engagement, so that technology-related cognitive economization, a reduction in cognitive and social-affective resources for non-human partners, takes the form of attenuation rather than absence. Alongside this attenuation, trust in the system tracked its reliability without exceeding it.

Convincing digital copies of professional selves, avatars that look, sound, and respond like a person, have become easier to produce with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). This paper reports work in progress on a postgraduate business subject at an Australian university, in which students explore professional identity by constructing, testing, and questioning AI representations of themselves. In a curriculum-embedded workshop, students choose between two equivalent activities: building an AI avatar from a self-authored knowledge base or writing a structured professional profile. Both ask students to decide deliberately what to share with, and withhold from, an AI system, then to test their representation against simulated professional scenarios before reflection and debrief. Drawing on postdigital perspectives, the design positions GenAI as neither threat nor solution but as a provocation for identity work. Both critical evaluation of technology and self-knowledge matter more when AI can convincingly represent a person. Preliminary findings from this first iteration, drawn from facilitator reflections and de-identified conversation logs, suggest that the pedagogical value of self-representing avatars lies in the critical questioning they provoke, rather than in their technical sophistication. The workshop offers a practical, adaptable model for critical and creative engagement with GenAI and professional identity.

Organizations must combine clear downward direction with upward employee voice, and the age diversity of contemporary workforces is often presented as making this balance harder to achieve. This article examines that claim through an integrative review of research on organizational communication, employee voice and silence, psychological safety, organizational justice, and generational diversity. The review covers the four cohorts that dominate today's workforce (Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z), considers Generation Alpha prospectively, and sets boundaries for its central constructs: multigenerational workplace, downward and upward communication, communication balance, and communication equilibrium. Searches combined communication-direction, voice, and generation terms, supplemented by citation tracing and targeted searches of African journal platforms; sources were screened against explicit inclusion criteria, synthesized through data reduction, display, comparison, and verification, and each claim was graded as established, supported, or conjectural. Meta-analytic and consensus evidence shows that differences between generational cohorts in work attitudes are small and confounded with age and period effects. The article therefore proposes a Generational Variation-Based Communication Equilibrium Model (CEM), which starts from age diversity but locates its communicative effects in five proximal sources of variation: career stage, hierarchical role, digital access, work arrangement, and cultural orientation. The model specifies one downward condition (directive clarity), two upward conditions (psychological safety and leadership responsiveness), and one bidirectional condition (channel diversity), which together sustain directional balance, a state in which decision-makers act on clear direction and accurate upward information. Five assumptions underpin the model, and equilibrium is maintained by a balancing responsiveness loop that counters a reinforcing spiral of silence. Eight propositions, with indicators, levels of analysis, and evidential status, set out a research agenda that prioritizes designs separating age, period, and cohort effects and theory built from sub-Saharan African organizations, treating their employees as agents of voice rather than deviations from Northern norms.

BETTER 2040 is an immersive, interactive symposium that invites participants to explore the technological, epistemic, and ethical disruptions reshaping higher education in the age of generative AI. Set within the fictional University of Banford, participants engage with realistic leadership scenarios, collaborative decision-making, and strategic design challenges to examine trust, pedagogical innovation, and institutional transformation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

The rapid expansion of shared e-scooter services has introduced a novel public health challenge, with rising injury rates reported globally. Existing epidemiological studies rely largely on retrospective hospital or police records, which lack data on pre-crash mechanisms. While naturalistic studies have begun to fill this gap, they have thus far relied on associational measures that may be biased by confounding. This study aims to quantify the causal effects of rider behavior and environmental factors on e-scooter safety–critical events (SCEs) using a formal causal inference framework. We conducted a case-control analysis within a naturalistic riding study of a public e-scooter service in Gothenburg, Sweden (2022–2023), drawing from 6868 trips. Our analysis included 61 SCEs (cases) and 183 randomly selected control events. We used directed acyclic graphs to identify confounders and applied the parametric g-formula weighted for exposure duration to estimate adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences. After adjustment, the risk of an SCE increased substantially for single-handed riding (RR = 5.5), riding through an intersection (RR = 3.8), and inexperience (RR = 2.8). Phone use was associated with an approximately threefold increase in risk (RR = 3.1), though this estimate was not statistically significant. Both rider behavior (e.g., inexperience, single-handed riding) and the built environment (e.g., intersections) are significant causal contributors to e-scooter crash risk. These findings provide evidence for a multi-level public health strategy that focuses on novice rider education, infrastructure modifications at intersections, and technological interventions to support riders during their trips.

Although Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is grounded in principles of inclusion, flexibility, and learner variability, its implementation in higher education can become reduced to procedural or checklist-driven approaches, creating a tension between its human-centred philosophy and institutional practice. This paper adopts a reflective approach to examine the implementation of UDL across selected courses at an Australian university, exploring how shared understandings of inclusive teaching were co-constructed through dialogue between academics and an educational developer. The reflective inquiry suggests that meaningful UDL implementation is less dependent on frameworks than on relational, dialogic engagement through which pedagogical meaning is negotiated in context. At a time when higher education is increasingly shaped by digital technologies and artificial intelligence, the paper argues for re-centring relationships, collaboration, and human judgement as the foundation of meaningful curriculum transformation. In doing so, it positions educational developers as knowledge architects who facilitate the co-construction of inclusive pedagogical practice and offers a relational perspective on UDL implementation that may inform educational developers and academics seeking to implement inclusive curriculum renewal within their own institutional contexts.

Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

documents.abstract: Graduate employability has become a strategic priority across higher education, yet development of employability capabilities often remains fragmented, positioned outside the curriculum through co-curricular activities or graduate attribute frameworks that lack developmental coherence (Jackson & Bridgstock, 2021). This poster asks: how can employability capabilities be scaffolded longitudinally through reflective practice and Work-Integrated Learning to develop professional identity and career resilience in AI-enabled professional contexts? It presents the curriculum design rationale for the Bachelor of Applied Business at UNSW College, commencing October 2026, demonstrating how digital infrastructure, systematic reflection, and authentic workplace learning build career-ready graduates who work critically with emerging technologies. The design positions reflection not as an isolated assessment task but as career development pedagogy, building metacognitive capability, professional identity, and adaptive resilience across three years. This draws on foundational theories of reflective practice (Schön, 1992) and transformative learning (Mezirow, 1991), integrated with contemporary scholarship on professional identity formation (Jackson, 2016, 2017) and career adaptability (Savickas & Porfeli, 2012). The scaffolded architecture moves from foundational self-awareness tasks in Year 1, through applied workplace reflection during industry placements in Year 2, to integrative professional identity synthesis in the Year 3 capstone—providing authentic contexts for capability development throughout the degree. This progression is enabled through Canvas LMS integrated with the Stackle reflective learning platform. Stackle creates a longitudinal ePortfolio where students document reflective entries across all courses, receive structured prompts aligned to developmental focus, and build a cumulative narrative of professional growth. The curriculum embeds industry engagement through industry-informed assessment tasks across 100% of courses, formal placements, and a capstone industry project. Reflective practice is explicitly connected to each WIL experience through Stackle, requiring students to analyse workplace challenges and articulate capability development—an approach shown to strengthen pre-professional identity formation (Jackson, 2017; Trede et al., 2012). The platform enables integrated feedback from academic supervisors and industry mentors, making capability development visible to students, educators, and potential employers. Embedding AI fluency as a professional capability is central to this design. Rather than treating generative AI as peripheral or threatening to assessment integrity, the curriculum positions AI literacy as essential to contemporary professional practice. Students engage with transparent AI disclosure practices in reflection, use AI tools critically to analyse workplace data, and develop ethical reasoning frameworks for AI use. Assessment structures centre human judgment and applied problem-solving—reflective analysis, workplace challenge responses, and professional presentations—requiring critical thinking about AI outputs rather than uncritical acceptance. This responds to contemporary debates about authentic assessment in AI-mediated learning environments (Bearman et al., 2023), positioning graduates as professionals who work with AI critically and ethically. This poster presents: (1) the theoretical framework; (2) the three-year reflective practice progression model; (3) the WIL integration strategy with 100% industry-informed assessment; and (4) design principles for embedding AI fluency. The contribution is a replicable framework for embedding employability longitudinally while leveraging digital infrastructure to support human agency in AI-augmented professional contexts.

documents.abstract: Australian universities are revising generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) guidance under strong pressure to assure learning, academic integrity and assessment quality. This concise paper reports a public-source mapping of GenAI policy, assessment guidance and student AI-literacy preparation across the 38 Universities Australia member universities. Using six TEQSA sources as contextual material, 100 university sources were coded by authority level, dominant public guidance approach, assessment model and student-facing literacy support. The public evidence shows diverse policy configurations: 18 universities used a structured framework, scale, tier or lane model, while eight relied mainly on assessment-specific rules. Student preparation was also prominent: 19 universities provided formal AI-specific learning opportunities, and 12 provided structured student hubs or toolkits. The findings suggest that GenAI policy can function as curriculum infrastructure rather than only academic-integrity compliance. The paper contributes to Human-Centred Learning Design by treating GenAI policy as learning design infrastructure that connects assessment authority, student trust, feedback expectations and AI literacy.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally altered how learners access, construct, and engage with knowledge. Existing discussions of GenAI literacy have largely emphasised operational competencies, such as prompt engineering, understanding AI capabilities, and ethical use. While these competencies remain important, they do not fully address the epistemic challenges arising from AI-mediated knowledge production. This paper proposes reframing GenAI literacy through the lens of epistemic agency; that is, learners’ capacity to critically evaluate, regulate, justify, and take responsibility for knowledge generated in collaboration with intelligent systems. Rather than viewing GenAI literacy as a collection of technical skills, this conceptual paper argues that its primary educational purpose is to cultivate learners who can exercise informed judgement in increasingly AI-mediated learning environments. Building on existing AI literacy scholarship and theories of epistemic agency, the paper introduces a conceptual framework comprising four interrelated dimensions: epistemic evaluation, epistemic regulation, epistemic responsibility, and epistemic autonomy. The framework provides a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding how GenAI literacy can move beyond operational competence towards fostering independent, reflective, and responsible knowledge construction.

Embodied foundation models produce impressive demonstrations, but executing long, complex tasks depends on software outside the model, just as in the ransition from ChatGPT to Codex. We call that software the embodied agent harness and divide it into planning, skill acquisition, memory, monitoring, and self-evolution. The papers come from robotics, machine learning, and embodied-AI venues, 2022--2026. About a fifth of the citations are preprints or non-archival manuscripts, mostly for new directions. Open problems remain in efficiency, robustness, generalizability, model availability, multi-robot orchestration, and evaluation.

Assessment in data visualisation courses too often rewards technical output over communicating substance. When visualisation is taught as a tool rather than a discipline, students learn to produce work that meets the brief but has little to say. This paper reports on a course redesign that addresses this gap through a human-centred assessment design grounded in evaluative judgement theory, treating evaluative judgement as a capability exercised by both students and markers. The redesign is structured around five elements addressing student ownership of project topics, portfolio assessment, descriptive capability levels, practitioner modelling, and creative freedom within a structured framework, implemented in a required course within a Master of Data Science program. Practitioner inquiry into the operation of this design in the presence of generative AI revealed that AI functioned not as a threat to academic integrity but as a mechanism that raised creative ambition, shifting the limiting factor from technical skill to evaluative judgement. Although situated in a data visualisation course, the contribution is broader. As generative AI makes technical production easier, helping students develop the capacity to recognise, justify, and communicate insight becomes the central challenge across higher education, and this paper suggests one way to address it.

The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has accelerated institutional investment in AI infrastructure, yet many universities continue to face difficulties translating institutional strategy into consistent subject-level teaching practice. This paper presents a School-level framework developed at an Australian university. The paper reports the design rationale, outputs and approved deployment model of the framework, including staff capability resources, configurable AI templates, disclosure mechanisms and governance processes. Informed by Educational Design Research and scholarship on organisational change in education, the paper argues that Schools can serve as meso-level environments that enact institutional AI strategy through resources and structures designed to support subject-level teaching practice. It contributes a meso-level governance model, six transferable design principles, and an operational framework intended to support responsible and human-centred AI-supported learning. Formal evaluation is planned following the pilot phase.

documents.abstract: Technical job interviews place computing students under pressure to demonstrate algorithmic and communication skills simultaneously under live observation, producing what we term the articulation gap. Existing preparation pathways provide only partial support: coding platforms ignore communication, coaching is economically inaccessible, and current AI simulators remain reactive. We present AIView, a multi-agent conversational platform that scaffolds integrated interview competencies. A LangGraph orchestrator coordinates specialised agents for question delivery and adaptive guidance alongside verbalisation monitors and an affect-aware tone layer, with assessments anchored in the SOLO taxonomy. An evaluation with 31 students showed high usability (SUS = 73.8), strong trust in AI feedback (M = 3.94), and high recommendation intent (M = 4.29). Participants valued personalised, code-aware feedback and a low-pressure learning environment. By fostering compassionate human-AI collaboration that supports creative problem solving and connection in a digital learning environment, AIView represents a step towards democratising access to career preparation through adaptive scaffolding.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. Boden supplies the criteria students apply when judging whether their output is genuinely novel, surprising and valuable; Kolb supplies the cycle through which that judgement is made repeatedly and acted upon. Without Boden, reflection has no object; without Kolb, the criteria are applied once and forgotten. Students work through Kolb’s (2011) four stages in their learning: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. These each serve a cumulative purpose in developing the students’ collaborative process with generative AI. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. Afterward, they reflect on that experience, considering questions about what skills they developed (or did not), whether the draft did what they wanted it to do, and how they felt about the AI tool use. Based on this reflection, they can then develop and express a personal set of beliefs on practical use of generative AI. Finally, they can try out a new approach based on these conclusions – which then become the next concrete experience. It is an ongoing and cyclical process of practical experimentation and personal reflection. The framework is adapted from the “Creativity and AI” module of Sage’s Digital Literacy course (Zaphir & Henrickson, in press). Its purpose is to be discipline agnostic; a framework which can be broadly applicable across cohorts and disciplines. Critical AI literacies require the development of students’ own ethical ideas and practical skills in using the tools; this process is designed to be adaptable in any context. Creativity has different implications and different applications in each discipline. AI can act as a useful collaborator if the user can state what and why they want to do it. Students will all benefit in the exercise of deliberately choosing which skills to offload and which to augment, and then reflecting on their choices with each use. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. Attendees will leave with the reflection prompts used at each stage and a one-page cycle template they can adapt to their own discipline and cohort.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been the focus of much attention in the higher education sector, both for its potential to support personalised and adaptive learning, but also due to the risk that students may outsource learning to it, leading to gaps in their professional or discipline competencies. This risk of cognitive offloading applies equally to learning how to learn, a skill set explored through studies of self-regulated learning (SRL). Two GenAI numeracy tutors were piloted at a regional Australian university as one component of a newly launched mathematics and statistics support centre, one focusing on medication calculations for Nursing students (NiNA), and the other on threshold numeracy skills for Education students (EdNA). Detailed analysis of students’ conversations with these agents using Zimmerman and Moylan’s 2009 SRL framework revealed extensive evidence of some elements of SRL such as strategic planning, task-specific strategies, and adaptive competence; trace evidence of other elements including self-efficacy and self-evaluation; and no evidence of the remaining elements. This study contributes an underrepresented qualitative perspective to the body of research into the crossover of GenAI and SRL and foreshadows avenues for further research and refinements in the design of GenAI numeracy tutors.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Esta pesquisa analisou a incorporação de um módulo multimodal de inteligência artificial (IA), o Acelerador de Catalogação, a um sistema de gestão de bibliotecas, com objetivo central de considerar o impacto dessa ferramenta na rotina de processamento técnico, avaliando a eficiência operacional, a precisão da extração de dados e a facilidade de uso, com especial atenção à preservação da soberania técnica do bibliotecário. Realizou-se um estudo de caso quali-quantitativo em ambiente real de trabalho, com 12 bibliotecários voluntários experientes em catalogação tradicional. Os dados quantitativos, extraídos automaticamente pelo sistema, compararam 52 registros do regime tradicional e 64 do regime assistido por IA; os dados qualitativos vieram de um fórum de diálogo colaborativo, contido como ferramenta do próprio software com recursos de interação e engajamento, este fórum foi subdividido em cinco eixos temáticos, tratado por análise de conteúdo. Os resultados evidenciaram uma redução média por título que caiu 32,5% (de 10 min 13 s para 6 min 54 s) e a completude aumentou 24,5% (de 23,6 para 29,4 campos preenchidos). A IA foi eficaz em tarefas mimeomórficas (ações mecânicas, repetitivas e estruturadas), enquanto as tarefas polimórficas, que exigem julgamento contextual, tratamento de exceções e adequação a políticas locais, permaneceram com o profissional, porém com sugestões do agente de IA. Observou-se maior incidência de edições posteriores ao cadastro no regime assistido (11 em 64 processos, contra 2 em 52), concentrada em um catalogador e em obras jurídicas. Os participantes descreveram a tecnologia como “assistente sob comando”, o que sustenta a curadoria humana como componente estrutural do fluxo. Concluiu-se que o ganho de eficiência convive com a preservação da autoridade técnica e do protagonismo do bibliotecário.
topics: Information Science, Archives and Information Policy

documents.abstract: This study examines how awareness of generative AI academic integrity policies shapes student anxiety, ethical reasoning, and writing practices in higher education. Drawing on a reflexive thematic analysis of student discourse from YouTube and Reddit, the study explores how detection-oriented governance frameworks are experienced and negotiated outside formal institutional contexts. Findings indicate that students do not primarily describe intentional rule-breaking; instead, they articulate experiences of surveillance, uncertainty, and adaptation within assessment systems perceived as inconsistent and adversarial. Three interrelated themes are identified: surveillance anxiety and defensive authorship; normative dissonance and moral negotiation of AI use; and cognitive offloading, systemic strain, and declining trust in assessment integrity. Across these themes, AI policy awareness is shown to shape not only behavioural responses but also students’ affective and epistemic relationships with writing, authorship, and institutional authority. The study argues that detection-first approaches risk intensifying anxiety and undermining trust without resolving underlying tensions in assessment design. It concludes that generative AI exposes structural fragilities in higher education, suggesting the need to reorient academic integrity governance toward design-led, transparent, and equity-sensitive approaches that prioritise learning, trust, and student experience.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human decision-making under uncertainty faces growing challenges from information-based threats that pose risks to human cognitive processes and behaviour. Although their potential harm is widely acknowledged, there remains no well-defined construct for characterising the degree to which information-based threats influence changes in human judgments and decision-making, impeding theoretical advancement, measurement, and effective countermeasure development. Here, we introduce a human cognitive security construct focused on linking information-based threats to observable outcomes to bridge field-level definitions with operational measures by drawing from core mechanisms related to information processing and decision-making. To connect the information environment to behaviour, we develop an integrative modelling framework that unifies Bayesian inference with affect-modulated decision valuation, capturing how cognitive resource allocation and affective valuation shape three core behavioural outcomes: veracity discernment, task-oriented actions, and information sharing. Through computational simulations, we demonstrate that this framework can explain canonical phenomena, including cognitive heuristics and incongruent veracity discernment and sharing behaviour, and we test model predictions against empirical data of the illusory truth effect (R² = 0.86). To guide future empirical examinations, we propose empirically grounded behavioural outcome measures of cognitive security and outline how environment-specific elements, characterised by data availability and ecological constraints, affect individuals’ cognitive security.
